title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
lead: Heat transfer and work are the two ways energy crosses the boundary of a system, and what stays behind is its internal energy. This section states the first law of thermodynamics, which is the conservation of energy written for those two transfers, fixes the signs of heat transfer into a system and work done by it, shows that the change in internal energy depends only on the state a system starts in and the state it ends in and not on the path between them, and applies the law to the human body, where food, heat transfer, work and stored fat keep the account.
objectives: Define the first law of thermodynamics.
Describe how conservation of energy relates to the first law of thermodynamics.
Identify instances of the first law of thermodynamics working in everyday situations, including biological metabolism.
Calculate changes in the internal energy of a system, after accounting for heat transfer and work done.
summary_html:
• The first law of thermodynamics is given as $\kdEint = \kQh - \kW$, where $\kdEint$ is the change in internal energy of a system, $\kQh$ is the net heat transfer (the sum of all heat transfer into and out of the system), and $\kW$ is the net work done (the sum of all work done on or by the system).
  • Both $\kQh$ and $\kW$ are energy in transit; only $\kdEint$ represents an independent quantity capable of being stored.
  • The internal energy $\kEint$ of a system depends only on the state of the system and not how it reached that state.
  • Metabolism of living organisms, and photosynthesis of plants, are specialized types of heat transfer, doing work, and internal energy of systems.
notes: The AP item on what happens inside a closed refrigerator or freezer is set in 15.5, which introduces the refrigerator, and the four problems the book leaves unkeyed are left out: the heat transfer from a system whose internal energy fell by 150 J, the system that does 4.50 × 10⁵ J of work with heat transfer in and out, the man who does 35.0 kJ of work at 5.00% efficiency, and the 1470-kJ cup of yogurt.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key. Problems 2, 4, 6 and 8 have no keyed answer and are left out: the heat transfer from a system whose internal energy decreased by 150 J while it did 30.0 J of work, the system that does 4.50 × 10⁵ J of work with 3.00 × 10⁶ J of heat transfer in and 8.00 × 10⁶ J out, the man who metabolizes food to do 35.0 kJ of work at 5.00% efficiency, and the 1470-kJ cup of yogurt. Problem 9 keys only part (a), so the card checks that number and carries the book’s own discussion of part (b) in its solution; Problem 7’s third part is set as the motor’s daily work, with the book’s comparison in the solution. Of the section’s six AP items, three are keyed and set as graded choices (the cylinder divided by a disk, the 300 J of work with −320 J of heat transfer, and the potato cannon); the billiard balls on springs and the snack burned off at 150 W have no key and are kept as open items with AI-written suggested approaches, marked as such; the item on what happens inside a closed refrigerator or freezer is answered by the refrigerator of 15.5 and is set there with source_section 15.1, unkeyed, with an AI-written approach. The suggested approaches to the seven conceptual questions are AI-written and marked. The chapter has no Check Your Understanding box, so nothing is set inline. Nothing is taken from another section. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: The first law of thermodynamics is the conservation-of-energy principle stated for a system where heat and work are the methods of transferring energy for a system in thermal equilibrium. Q represents the net heat transfer—it is the sum of all heat transfers into and out of the system. Q is positive for net heat transfer into the system. W is the total work done on and by the system. W is positive when more work is done by the system than on it. The change in the internal energy of the system, ΔE_int, is related to heat and work by the first law of thermodynamics, ΔE_int = Q − W.

Two different processes produce the same change in a system. (a) A total of 15.00 J of heat transfer occurs into the system, while work takes out a total of 6.00 J. The change in internal energy is ΔE_int = Q − W = 9.00 J. (b) Heat transfer removes 150.00 J from the system while work puts 159.00 J into it, producing an increase of 9.00 J in internal energy. If the system starts out in the same state in (a) and (b), it will end up in the same final state in either case—its final state is related to internal energy, not how that energy was acquired.

(a) The first law of thermodynamics applied to metabolism. Heat transferred out of the body (Q) and work done by the body (W) remove internal energy, while food intake replaces it. (Food intake may be considered as work done on the body.) (b) Plants convert part of the radiant heat transfer in sunlight to stored chemical energy, a process called photosynthesis.

exercises.prompt: Describe the photo of the tea kettle at the beginning of this section in terms of heat transfer, work done, and internal energy. How is heat being transferred? What is the work done and what is doing it? How does the kettle maintain its internal energy?

answer.solution: Take the kettle and the water in it as the system. Heat is transferred into the system from the burner of the stove, by conduction through the metal of the kettle into the water and by the hot gases and radiation of the flame reaching the underside of the kettle, and this heat transfer is what raises the internal energy of the water until it boils. The work is done by the water vapor: as the water turns to steam it expands enormously, pushes the air out of the way at the spout, and forces its way through the whistle, setting it sounding, so the expanding steam is doing work on its surroundings against the pressure of the atmosphere. The kettle maintains its internal energy because the heat transfer in from the stove keeps pace with what leaves; while the water boils its temperature stays fixed, and the energy the stove supplies goes into turning water into vapor, which carries energy away through the spout, and into the work the steam does. If the burner were turned off, the heat transfer in would stop, the work and the heat transfer out would continue for a while, and the internal energy of the kettle would fall, which is why it stops whistling.

exercises.prompt: The first law of thermodynamics and the conservation of energy, as discussed in Conservation of Energy, are clearly related. How do they differ in the types of energy considered?

answer.solution: The law of conservation of energy says that the total energy of a system, in all of its forms, is constant unless energy is transferred into or out of the system, and in Chapter 7 the forms it kept track of were mainly the kinetic and potential energies of objects as a whole, with work as the way energy was transferred. The first law of thermodynamics is the same principle written for a particular set of forms and transfers: the energy stored is the internal energy, the kinetic and potential energies of the atoms and molecules of the system rather than of the object as a whole, and the two ways energy crosses the boundary are heat transfer, which conservation of energy in Chapter 7 did not single out, and work. So the first law considers internal energy where the earlier statement considered mechanical energy, and it adds heat transfer to work as a means of transfer. Neither law says anything the other contradicts; the first law is conservation of energy in the form that is most useful when heat transfer and work are what is going on.

exercises.prompt: Heat transfer $\kQh$ and work done $\kW$ are always energy in transit, whereas internal energy $\kEint$ is energy stored in a system. Give an example of each type of energy, and state specifically how it is either in transit or resides in a system.

answer.solution: Heat transfer: the energy that passes from a hot stove burner into a pan of water because the burner is hotter than the water. It is in transit because it exists only while the temperature difference drives it across the boundary between burner and water; once it has arrived it is simply part of the water’s energy and no longer heat. Work: the energy a bicycle pump delivers to the air in a tire as the piston pushes the air through a distance. It too is in transit, because it is energy passing from the pump to the air during the stroke, and nothing in the tire afterward can be pointed to as work. Internal energy: the energy the warm air in the tire now holds, the kinetic energy of its molecules and the potential energy of their interactions. It resides in the system because it is a property of the air in its present state, the same however the air came to be warm, and it stays there until heat transfer or work carries some of it away.

exercises.prompt: How do heat transfer and internal energy differ? In particular, which can be stored as such in a system and which cannot?

answer.solution: Heat transfer is a process, the passing of energy from one body to another because their temperatures differ, and internal energy is a quantity a system possesses, the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules. Internal energy can be stored, and is: a system in a given state has a definite internal energy, and the first law keeps the account of how heat transfer and work change it. Heat transfer cannot be stored as such. Once energy has entered a system by heat transfer it is internal energy like any other, indistinguishable from energy that entered as work, so a system has no heat in it to be stored, only the internal energy that heat transfer may have raised. That is why the book says heat transfer rather than heat, to keep the process from being mistaken for a thing a body holds.

exercises.prompt: If you run down some stairs and stop, what happens to your kinetic energy and your initial gravitational potential energy?

answer.solution: Both end up as internal energy, most of it thermal. As you descend, gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy, and your muscles, tendons and the soles of your shoes do negative work at every step to keep you from speeding up, turning that kinetic energy into thermal energy in your legs, your shoes, the stairs and the air, with a little going into sound. When you stop at the bottom the last of your kinetic energy goes the same way. Your body is slightly warmer than before and so are the stairs, and that extra internal energy is then transferred to the surroundings as heat. None of it can be recovered as potential energy by itself; you cannot get back up the stairs by cooling down, which is one of the irreversible processes the section describes.

exercises.prompt: Give an explanation of how food energy (calories) can be viewed as molecular potential energy (consistent with the atomic and molecular definition of internal energy).

answer.solution: The internal energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules, and the potential energy part includes the energy stored in the way atoms are bound to one another within molecules. A food molecule such as a sugar is an arrangement of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms held together by electric forces, and that arrangement has more potential energy than the same atoms would have if they were rearranged into carbon dioxide and water. Metabolism is the oxidation that makes that rearrangement, and the difference in potential energy is released, to be transferred as heat, to do work, or to be stored. So the Calories printed on a food label are a measure of molecular potential energy: the energy that the atoms of the food would give up on being rearranged into lower-energy molecules, which is the same energy a calorimeter measures by burning the food.

exercises.prompt: Identify the type of energy transferred to your body in each of the following as either internal energy, heat transfer, or doing work: (a) basking in sunlight; (b) eating food; (c) riding an elevator to a higher floor.

answer.solution: (a) Basking in sunlight is heat transfer: the Sun is hotter than your skin and its radiation carries energy into your body because of that temperature difference, just as sunlight warms the air in a bicycle tire. (b) Eating food adds internal energy: the food carries chemical potential energy of its molecules into the body, and the section notes that since metabolism releases it in an oxidation process, food input may be counted as work done on the body in the first law, but the energy arrives stored in the food and not as heat. (c) Riding an elevator to a higher floor is work done on you: the floor of the elevator pushes up on your feet through the distance you rise, and the work it does increases your gravitational potential energy, not your internal energy, which is why you arrive no warmer than you left.

exercises.prompt: A cylinder is divided in half by a movable disk in the middle. Each half is filled with an equal number of gas molecules, but one half is at a higher temperature than the other. Which choice best describes what happens next?

options: The high temperature side expands, compressing the low temperature side.
Heat moves from hot to cold, so the low temperature side will gradually increase in temperature and expand
(b) happens quickly, but after that (c) happens more slowly.
answer.hint: Two things happen on different time scales. The gas at the higher temperature has the higher pressure and pushes the disk at once, which is work; the temperature difference then drives a slower transfer through the disk, which is heat.

exercises.prompt: Imagine a solid material at the molecular level as consisting of a bunch of billiard balls connected to each other by springs (this is actually a surprisingly useful approximation). If we have two blocks of the same material, but in one the billiard balls are shaking back and forth on their springs a great deal, and in the other they are barely moving, which block is at the higher temperature? Using what you know about conservation of momentum in collisions, describe which block will transfer energy to the other, and justify your answer.

answer.solution: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms and molecules, so the block whose balls are shaking a great deal is the one at the higher temperature; its internal energy, the sum of the kinetic energy of the balls and the potential energy stored in the stretched and compressed springs, is the larger. Now bring the two blocks into contact so that the balls at the surface of one collide with the balls at the surface of the other. In a collision between a fast ball and a slow one, momentum is conserved and kinetic energy is shared out; on average the faster ball loses kinetic energy and the slower one gains it, as the collisions of Chapter 8 show, and a slow ball hit by a fast one recoils with more energy than it had. Collision after collision, energy therefore passes from the block whose balls move a great deal to the block whose balls barely move, never the other way on balance, and it spreads inward through the springs. This is heat transfer at the molecular level, driven by the temperature difference, and it continues until the average kinetic energy of the balls, which is to say the temperature, is the same in both blocks.

exercises.prompt: A system has 300 J of work done on it, and has a heat transfer of -320 J. Compared to prior to these processes, the internal energy is:

answer.hint: Work done on the system is negative work done by the system, so $\kW = -300\ \text{J}$, and the heat transfer is already given with its sign.

exercises.prompt: Find a snack or drink item in the classroom, or at your next meal. Find the total Calories (kilocalories) in the item, and calculate how long it would take exercising at 150 W (moderately, climbing stairs) at 20% efficiency to burn off this energy.

answer.solution: Read the Calories from the label and convert them to joules: one food Calorie is one kilocalorie, and $1\ \text{kcal} = 4186\ \text{J}$, so the food energy is $E = (\text{Calories})(4186\ \text{J})$. An efficiency of 20% means that only one fifth of the internal energy the body uses up appears as work, the rest leaving as heat transfer, so burning off the whole of the snack’s energy requires doing work $\kW = 0.20E$. Exercising at 150 W does 150 J of work each second, so the time needed is $t = \kW/P = 0.20E/(150\ \text{W})$. For a snack labelled a few hundred Calories the energy is around a million joules and the time comes out at something over twenty minutes of stair climbing, which is the point of the exercise: a small snack is a long climb. Note that the body’s own metabolic rate at rest is not counted here, only the work of the exercise.

exercises.prompt: A potato cannon has the fuel combusted, generating a lot of heat and pressure, which launch a potato. The combustion process _____ the internal energy, while launching the potato _____ the internal energy of the potato cannon.

answer.hint: Ask of each step whether energy is added to the gas in the cannon or taken from it. Combustion releases energy into the gas; launching the potato is work the gas does on the potato.

exercises.prompt: What is the change in internal energy of a car if you put 12.0 gal of gasoline into its tank? The energy content of gasoline is $1.3\times10^{8}\ \text{J/gal}$. All other factors, such as the car’s temperature, are constant.

answer.hint: The gasoline enters the car as chemical potential energy, which is internal energy, and nothing else about the car changes, so the change in internal energy is the energy content of the fuel added.

exercises.prompt: A system does $1.80\times10^{8}\ \text{J}$ of work while $7.50\times10^{8}\ \text{J}$ of heat transfer occurs to the environment. What is the change in internal energy of the system assuming no other changes (such as in temperature or by the addition of fuel)?

answer.hint: Heat transfer to the environment is out of the system, so $\kQh$ is negative, and work done by the system makes $\kW$ positive; both take internal energy away.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a woman does 500 J of work and 9500 J of heat transfer occurs into the environment in the process. (a) What is the decrease in her internal energy, assuming no change in temperature or consumption of food? (That is, there is no other energy transfer.) (b) What is her efficiency?

parts.hint: Take her body as the system: the heat transfer is out, so $\kQh = -9500\ \text{J}$, and the work is done by her, so $\kW = +500\ \text{J}$.
Efficiency is the useful work output divided by the energy consumed, and here the energy consumed is the internal energy she has lost.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the average metabolic rate in watts of a man who metabolizes 10,500 kJ of food energy in one day? (b) What is the maximum amount of work in joules he can do without breaking down fat, assuming a maximum efficiency of 20.0%? (c) Compare his work output with the daily output of a 187-W (0.250-horsepower) motor.

parts.hint: A rate is an energy divided by a time; one day is 86,400 s.
Without breaking down fat, the internal energy he can spend in a day is the food energy he took in, and at most 20.0% of it comes out as work.

parts.part: (c), the work done by the motor in a day
parts.hint: The motor’s power times the seconds in a day gives its work, and the comparison is the ratio of the two.

answer.solution: (a) 122 W (b) $2.10\times10^{6}\ \text{J}$ (c) Work done by the motor is $1.61\times10^{7}\ \text{J}$; thus the motor produces 7.67 times the work done by the man

exercises.prompt: (a) A woman climbing the Washington Monument metabolizes $6.00\times10^{2}\ \text{kJ}$ of food energy. If her efficiency is 18.0%, how much heat transfer occurs to the environment to keep her temperature constant? (b) Discuss the amount of heat transfer found in (a). Is it consistent with the fact that you quickly warm up when exercising?

answer.hint: Her efficiency says how much of the 600 kJ becomes work; to keep her temperature constant, the rest of the internal energy she spends must leave as heat transfer.
answer.solution: (a) 492 kJ (b) This amount of heat is consistent with the fact that you warm quickly when exercising. Since the body is inefficient, the excess heat produced must be dissipated through sweating, breathing, etc.
